title: What is data engineering — the work of building systems that collect, store, and prepare data so that others (analysts, data scientists, ML models) can use it easily and quickly.

s1_definition.profdef: Data engineering is the discipline of designing, building, and operating the systems and pipelines that collect raw data from many sources, move it reliably, clean and transform it, and store it in a shape that downstream consumers like analysts, data scientists, dashboards, and machine learning models can query quickly. A data engineer owns ingestion, storage, transformation, orchestration, data quality, and the reliability and cost of all of that at scale.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India generates a flood of raw events all day — Rajesh swipes his card, Priya transfers rent, ATMs spit out cash, loans get approved. That raw data is messy and scattered across dozens of systems. A data engineer is like the person who builds the pipes, filters, and warehouses of the bank's "data plumbing": they collect every drop of raw data, clean out the dirt, and store it neatly in labelled tanks so that the analytics team can instantly answer "how much did Rajesh spend last month?" without digging through the raw sewage themselves.
s1_definition.oneliner: Data engineering builds the reliable plumbing that turns messy raw data into clean, query-ready data for everyone else.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Data engineering is the discipline of designing, building, and operating the systems and pipelines that collect raw data from many sources, move it reliably, clean and transform it, and store it in a shape that downstream consumers like analysts, data scientists, dashboards, and machine learning models can query quickly. A data engineer owns ingestion, storage, transformation, orchestration, data quality, and the reliability and cost of all of that at scale.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India generates a flood of raw events all day — Rajesh swipes his card, Priya transfers rent, ATMs spit out cash, loans get approved. That raw data is messy and scattered across dozens of systems. A data engineer is like the person who builds the pipes, filters, and warehouses of the bank's "data plumbing": they collect every drop of raw data, clean out the dirt, and store it neatly in labelled tanks so that the analytics team can instantly answer "how much did Rajesh spend last month?" without digging through the raw sewage themselves.

**One line to remember:** Data engineering builds the reliable plumbing that turns messy raw data into clean, query-ready data for everyone else.

sections.s2_technical:
Data engineering sits upstream of analytics and machine learning. The core job is to make trustworthy data available at the right place, in the right shape, at the right time. It breaks down into a few repeating responsibilities.

The first responsibility is ingestion — getting data out of source systems. Sources include transactional databases (the production PostgreSQL holding accounts), event streams (Kafka topics carrying card swipes), external APIs (a credit bureau like CIBIL), and files (end-of-day settlement CSVs from an exchange). In Java you might read a stream with a Kafka consumer: `consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))` returns a batch of `ConsumerRecord` objects, each one a raw transaction event you then hand to the pipeline.

The second responsibility is storage. Raw data often lands first in a cheap data lake (object storage like S3), then refined data moves into a warehouse (Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery) optimized for analytical queries. Choosing row-oriented versus column-oriented storage, and formats like Parquet, is a storage decision a data engineer makes constantly.

The third responsibility is transformation — cleaning nulls, standardizing currencies, joining a transaction to its account, deduplicating, and aggregating. This is the "T" in ETL. A small example of a transform expressed in Java-like pseudocode is filtering out invalid rows: `txns.stream().filter(t -> t.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0).toList()` keeps only positive-amount transactions.

The fourth responsibility is orchestration — scheduling and sequencing these steps so that the "clean transactions" job only runs after the "load raw transactions" job succeeds. Tools like Apache Airflow express this as a directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies and retries.

The fifth responsibility, and the one that separates a junior from a senior, is reliability and quality. A senior data engineer thinks about idempotency (re-running a job must not double-count Rajesh's transfer), schema evolution (a new column appears tomorrow), late and out-of-order data, backfills, monitoring, cost, and data contracts with upstream teams. In banking this matters enormously because a wrong number is not just an inconvenience — it can be a regulatory breach or a customer seeing the wrong balance.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces millions of raw transaction events a day, and they arrive as messy objects with missing fields, wrong signs, and duplicates. The analytics team cannot use this raw sewage directly. This is exactly the problem data engineering solves — we build a pipeline that ingests raw events, cleans them, and loads clean records ready for reporting.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the same transfer event arrives twice because a producer retried. If we naively count both, Rajesh's spending looks doubled. This is exactly why data engineers build idempotent, deduplicating pipelines — each unique transaction id is counted once.

Problem 3 — The business wants a simple daily summary: total spend per account. Raw events alone do not answer that. This is exactly the transform-and-aggregate step of ETL — we group clean transactions by account and sum them.

The mini-project is a small ETL pipeline. `RawTransaction` is the dirty input record. `TransactionPipeline` is the engine with three stages: `extract()` produces raw records, `transform()` cleans and deduplicates them into `CleanTransaction` objects, and `load()` aggregates per account and prints the warehouse-ready summary. `AccountSummary` holds the final per-account total. The demo runs Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) through the full pipeline including a duplicate and an invalid record.

sections.s5_journey:
The input data is six raw transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), including one duplicate (TXN-2 twice), one null-amount record (TXN-4), and one negative-amount record (TXN-5).

Step 1 — Extract. The pipeline pulls all six raw records from the source. At this point the data lives in a list of `RawTransaction` objects and nothing has been cleaned. Good and bad records sit side by side.

Step 2 — Transform, validity check. The pipeline walks each record and drops TXN-4 (null amount) and TXN-5 (negative amount), logging a warning for each. The data shrinks to four candidate records.

Step 3 — Transform, deduplication. The pipeline tracks seen transaction ids in a set. When the second TXN-2 appears, `seen.add` returns false, so it is dropped as a duplicate. Now three clean records remain: TXN-1, TXN-2, TXN-3.

Step 4 — Load, aggregation. The pipeline groups the clean records by account. Rajesh's TXN-1 (1200) and TXN-2 (800) sum to 1800 across two transactions. Priya's TXN-3 sums to 5000 across one transaction.

Step 5 — Output. The per-account summary is printed as the warehouse-ready result. The raw messy input became two clean aggregate rows.

```
INFO: EXTRACT stage: pulling raw transactions from source
INFO: TRANSFORM stage: cleaning and deduplicating
WARNING: Dropping duplicate record TXN-2
WARNING: Dropping invalid record TXN-4
WARNING: Dropping invalid record TXN-5
INFO: LOAD stage: aggregating per account for the warehouse
INFO: === WAREHOUSE-READY SUMMARY ===
INFO: SAV2001 total=2000.00 count=2
INFO: CUR3001 total=5000.00 count=1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source: 6 raw transaction events
    │
    ▼
  EXTRACT
    │ list of RawTransaction (TXN-1..TXN-5, incl dupe + 2 invalid)
    ▼
  TRANSFORM
    ├─ drop invalid: TXN-4 (null), TXN-5 (negative)
    ├─ drop duplicate: second TXN-2
    │ result: TXN-1, TXN-2, TXN-3 (clean)
    ▼
  LOAD (aggregate by account)
    ├─ SAV2001: 1200 + 800 = 2000  (2 txns)
    └─ CUR3001: 5000             (1 txn)
    ▼
  Warehouse: account_daily_summary
  SAV2001 → 2000.00 | CUR3001 → 5000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Data engineering is the discipline of building and operating the systems that collect raw data from many sources, move it reliably, clean and transform it, and store it in a shape that analysts, data scientists, and machine learning models can query quickly and trust. A data engineer owns the whole pipeline: ingestion, storage, transformation, orchestration, data quality, and the reliability and cost of all of it at scale. In practice we sit upstream of the analytics and ML teams and our job is to make trustworthy data available at the right place, in the right shape, at the right time.

The work breaks into a few repeating responsibilities. Ingestion is getting data out of source systems, whether that is a transactional database, a Kafka event stream, an external API, or a nightly file. Storage is deciding where data lands, typically a cheap data lake first and then a column-oriented warehouse for fast analytics. Transformation is the cleaning, standardizing, joining, deduplicating, and aggregating that turns raw records into usable ones. Orchestration is scheduling and sequencing these steps with dependencies and retries so that a downstream job only runs after its upstream succeeds.

What separates a senior data engineer is obsession with reliability and quality. I always think about idempotency so that re-running a job never double-counts a transfer, schema evolution so a new column tomorrow does not break the pipeline, late and out-of-order data, backfills, monitoring, and clear data contracts with upstream teams.

In my project at the National Bank of India I built exactly this kind of pipeline for transaction data. Raw transaction events arrive messy, with nulls, wrong signs, and duplicates from producer retries. My pipeline extracts the raw records, transforms them by dropping invalid rows and deduplicating by transaction id, and loads a clean per-account daily summary into the warehouse. The reason this matters so much in a bank is that a wrong number is never just an inconvenience — it can mean a customer sees the wrong balance or we breach a regulatory report, so the pipeline is designed to be correct and safely re-runnable first, and fast second.

---

keyPoints: Data engineering: build pipelines to collect, transform, serve data
ETL: Extract, Transform, Load — move data from source to target
Data lake: raw storage (S3, ADLS). Data warehouse: structured (Redshift, BigQuery)
